confirmed: Read all 1,091 markdown lines, including appendices and references. The PDF has 48 pages with Supplementary Information on pp. 24–48; title/authors match and no manuscript date or version number is printed. The undated OSF-preprint version description is supported (PDF pp. 1, 24–48; retrieval.json, c205).

Sample 1 crosses task with AI chat versus solo within people and states counterbalancing, but never specifies randomized condition order. Retain randomized = not_stated, design_class = other, and core/criterion 1 = unclear; the false checker flag denotes unconfirmed randomization, not proof of nonrandom allocation (PDF pp. 16, 33–35; whole-document assignment check).

Samples 2–3 provide common ChatGPT/Gemini access and analyze measured CD and observed median-split groups; Sample 4 uses existing WildChat conversations. Observational study/context classifications are supported (PDF pp. 17–18, 35–38, 40–42).

Table S6 gives analytic N = 234, 205, 157, and 1,941 for Samples 1–4. The first three count people and exceed 50; Sample 4 counts user proxies. No randomized counts or separate Sample 1 condition-specific analyzed counts are reported (PDF p. 43, Table S6; pp. 33, 35, 37, 42).

Sample 1's 413 retained chats are task observations. Sample 2 has 205 people, 195 with complete individual-difference data, 656 scored chat transcripts, and 655 complete product responses; the separate five-rater panels are scorers (PDF pp. 6–7, 16–17, 33, 35).

Sample 3 reports 220 recruited, 168 completers, 157 after exclusions, and 422 task observations. Zero-message task observations were excluded from CD analyses, and participants with no AI engagement across all tasks were excluded entirely; these are not randomized counts (PDF p. 37, Participants).

WildChat counts match: 6,290 conversations/2,053 user identifiers; 5,772 product-scored conversations/1,941 analyzed users. The form correctly states the limitations of hashed-IP identity proxies and LLM-selected assistant product turns (PDF pp. 17–18, 41–42).

S1-O1 reported statistics match: title paired-samples dz = 0.82, design dz = 2.03, both p < .001; GPT-4.1, Qwen 3.5-397B, and Grok-3 score products on a 10–50 novelty/effectiveness scale (PDF pp. 10, 16, 35).

S1-O2 statistics/directions match: design chat .500 versus solo .338, d = 1.10; title chat .255 versus solo .297, d = −0.25. These are printed similarity effects without sign reversal; the exact independent analysis unit remains unstated (PDF pp. 10, 35).
S2-O1 matches: human-only CFA latent r = .30, p < .001, N = 205; separate five-rater panels, a 1–5 scale for both constructs, and task scores averaged within people (PDF pp. 8, 33).

The one-line finding correctly reports fixed-effects r = .28, 95% CI [.25, .32], N = 2,537. Figure 2 combines CD–creativity correlations from the paper's own four samples, including user proxies, not randomized AI-assistance effects. This is not a literature synthesis; synthesis defaults are appropriate (PDF pp. 7–8, Figure 2; p. 42).
summary: The recorded statistics and sample counts match the PDF, with WildChat counts representing hashed-IP users, but the form omits substantive outcomes and needs preregistration, funding, data/code, and outcome-metadata corrections. No randomized people study is confirmed: Sample 1 states counterbalancing without random order allocation, so core eligibility remains unclear and the measured-CD associations remain observational.
